name: Māori King movement
info: The Māori King movement, the Kīngitanga, arose among iwi of the central North Island of New Zealand in the 1850s to halt the alienation of Māori land through a Māori monarch; it was crowned in 1858 and continues today.

facts.where: New Zealand's North Island: Waikato, the King Country of the Ngāti Maniapoto, and Taranaki; its headquarters is Tūrangawaewae Marae at Ngāruawāhia.
facts.period: Rūnanga revived around 1853; Pōtatau Te Wherowhero crowned in 1858; the invasion of the Waikato from 1863 and Tāwhiao's exile of about 20 years; the Kauhanganui from 1892; the monarchs from Mahuta (1894) to Nga wai hono i te po (2024).
facts.figures: Tāmihana Te Rauparaha, who first proposed a Māori kingdom; Wiremu Tamihana, the kingmaker; the kings Pōtatau Te Wherowhero, Matutaera Tāwhiao, Mahuta, Te Rata and Korokī; Queen Te Atairangikaahu; King Tūheitia; Queen Nga wai hono i te po; Te Puea Hērangi, chief organiser.
facts.outcome: Defeat at Ōrākau in 1864 and the confiscation of 486,500 hectares of Waikato land; a movement that endures as a non-constitutional monarchy outside the New Zealand government, headed today by Nga wai hono i te po.

t: The Kīngitanga arose in the 1850s from Māori meetings that sought to unite iwi against the sale of their land, at a time when the number of European colonists was increasing rapidly.

Pōtatau Te Wherowhero was crowned at Ngāruawāhia in 1858, and the movement took on the appearance of an alternative government, with its own flag, newspaper, bank, councillors, magistrates and law enforcement.
The colonial government invaded the Waikato in 1863, 486,500 hectares were confiscated, and the movement survived in the King Country; the Māori monarchy now operates outside New Zealand law.
dyk: In July 1881 King Tāwhiao and 70 followers laid down their guns at Alexandra and placed beside them 70 roasted pigeons and a fantail, explaining, "This means peace."
ev: A meeting at Manawapou in south Taranaki, attended by as many as 2000 Māori leaders, hears calls for concerted opposition to land sales
Pōtatau Te Wherowhero is crowned as the first Māori king at Ngāruawāhia
Governor Grey issues an ultimatum on 9 July and troops invade the Waikato three days later
Defeat at Ōrākau drives the Kingites into the Ngāti Maniapoto region, which becomes known as the King Country
Tāwhiao and 70 followers lay down their guns at Alexandra as a sign of peace
Tāwhiao sets up the Kauhanganui, a Kīngitanga parliament, at Maungakawa
Police arrest men at Te Paina who failed to report for military duty under conscription
Nga wai hono i te po is announced as the eighth monarch after the death of King Tūheitia

sections.background:
From the early 1850s, North Island Māori came under increasing pressure to satisfy the demand of European settler farmers for arable land. Settlers expanded their production by burning forest and fern and planting grass seed in the ashes. Some influential chiefs, including Te Rauparaha, opposed land sales in the 1840s, a stand that culminated in the 1843 Wairau Affray. The view became more widespread in the following decade, when the Pākehā (European) population grew to outnumber Māori and the colonial government's Native Land Purchase Department adopted unscrupulous methods, among them offers to chiefs or small groups of owners.

Deals with individual Māori or groups that did not represent majority interests also dragged Māori into disputes with one another. As the white frontier encroached further, many became concerned that their land, and race, would soon be overrun. Around 1853 Māori revived the ancient tribal rūnanga, chiefly war councils, where land issues were raised, and in May 1854 a large meeting at Manawapou in south Taranaki, attracting as many as 2000 Māori leaders, heard speakers urge concerted opposition to selling land.

The meetings gave an important forum to Tāmihana Te Rauparaha, a Christian convert and son of Te Rauparaha, who had visited England in 1851 and been presented to Queen Victoria. He returned with the idea of a Māori kingdom, with one king ruling over all iwi (tribes), and used the rūnanga to secure the agreement of influential North Island chiefs.
sections.aims:
The kotahitanga, or unity movement, aimed to bring to Māori the unity that was an obvious strength among the Europeans. It was believed that by having a monarch who could claim status similar to that of Queen Victoria, Māori would be able to deal with Pākehā on equal footing. The movement also intended to establish a system of law and order in Māori communities, to which the Auckland government had so far shown little interest. Its central purpose was to halt the alienation of Māori land.

Wiremu Tamihana, called the kingmaker, set out the Kīngitanga's key concern in a letter to Governor Thomas Gore Browne at the close of the First Taranaki War in 1861. He said the Waikato iwi had never signed the Treaty of Waitangi and that Māori were a separate nation. "I do not desire to cast the Queen from this island, but from own piece (of land). I am to be the person to overlook my own piece," he wrote.

Pōtatau Te Wherowhero, in his acceptance speech, stressed the spirit of unity symbolised by the kingship and called on his people to "hold fast to love, to the law, and to faith in God." He envisaged a conjoint administration in which he ruled in territory still under Māori customary title while the Governor ruled in areas acquired by the Crown, and he named Maungatautari as the boundary between the two.
sections.events:
In February 1857 Wiremu Tamihana, a chief of the Ngāti Hauā iwi, circulated a proposal to appoint as king the elderly and high-ranking Waikato chief Te Wherowhero, after several other candidates had declined. Te Wherowhero accepted in September 1857 and was crowned at Ngāruawāhia in June 1858. The movement acquired a flag, a council of state, a code of laws, a "King's Resident Magistrate", police, a surveyor and a newspaper, Te Hokioi. Governor Browne watched with concern, writing that a separate nationality would "end sooner or later in collision". Pōtatau died on 25 June 1860 and was succeeded by his son Matutaera Tāwhiao.

Hostilities over land in Taranaki spread into the New Zealand Wars. Governor Browne regarded the Kīngitanga stance as disloyalty, and his plans for an invasion of the Waikato were fuelled in large part by a wish to uphold "the Queen's supremacy". His successor Sir George Grey told a Māori gathering in December 1861 that the King movement was bad and should be abandoned. On 9 July 1863 Grey issued an ultimatum that all Māori living between Auckland and the Waikato take an oath of allegiance to Queen Victoria or be expelled south of the Waikato River. Troops invaded three days later.

Kingite forces fought a defensive war but were unable to prevail over a full-time professional army with almost unlimited manpower and firepower. After their defeat at Ōrākau in 1864 they withdrew into the territory of Ngāti Maniapoto, which became known as the King Country, and Tāwhiao declared that Europeans risked death if they crossed the aukati, or boundary, of the confiscated land.
sections.people:
Tāmihana Te Rauparaha first brought the idea of a Māori kingdom from England, and Wiremu Tamihana of Ngāti Hauā, the "kingmaker", proposed Te Wherowhero as king. Historian Keith Sinclair claimed that "moderates" aligned themselves with Wiremu Tamihana and "anti-European extremists" followed the Ngāti Maniapoto chief and warlord Rewi Maniapoto; Belich and Vincent O'Malley dispute this, saying both factions were driven by shared objectives and that historians had exaggerated the divisions.

Tāwhiao renounced war, declaring 1867–68 the "year of the lamb" and "year of peace", and spent 20 years in exile. Te Kooti, a Ringatū prophet and guerrilla leader, challenged him in 1869 and 1870 to resume hostilities. Mahuta, born about 1854, took an interest in politics and sat on the Legislative Council and Executive Council from 1903. Te Puea Hērangi, his niece, became chief organiser for the movement in 1911, a role she held until her death in 1952, and later developed Tūrangawaewae marae. She rejected a proposal to make her monarch, believing Korokī was the rightful heir.

The fifth king, Korokī, was crowned in 1933 and accepted the role reluctantly. Te Atairangikaahu, his daughter, was elected the first Māori Queen in 1966 and reigned for 40 years, the longest of any monarch. Her son Tūheitia was sworn in on 21 August 2006, and on 5 September 2024 his daughter Nga wai hono i te po was announced as the next monarch.
sections.outcomes:
The confiscation of 486,500 hectares of land, including fertile areas under cultivation, burial sites and areas inhabited for centuries, was a bitter blow for Waikato Māori. Recognition of the first king had not been immediate: Pōtatau's role was strongly embraced only by Waikato Māori, and by the time of Mahuta's coronation support had declined, its followers limited mainly to the Tainui iwi in Waikato and Ngāti Maniapoto from the King Country. Tāwhiao refused the government's peace terms in 1878, and his petition to the Crown in London in 1884 was refused an audience with the Queen.

Throughout Mahuta's years as king, Waikato was mired in economic and social depression. Many Māori were landless and destitute because of confiscations, and the area had severe health problems. Te Rata's delegation to England in 1914 gained an audience with King George V but only the assurance that its claims would be referred back to the New Zealand Government.

In the First World War Te Rata discouraged Waikato enlistment. Te Puea explained: "They tell us to fight for king and country. We've got a King, but we haven't got a country. That's been taken off us." On 11 July 1918 police arrived at Te Paina and arrested men who had failed to report for military duty; they were taken to Narrow Neck army camp in Auckland and repeatedly punished for refusing to wear uniform, and 111 remained in confinement until May 1919. Pākehā widely regarded the Kīngitanga as seditious traitors and German sympathisers.
sections.legacy:
The Māori monarch operates in a non-constitutional capacity outside the New Zealand government, without explicit legal or judicial power. The monarchs are not recognised by New Zealand law or by many Māori iwi, though they are paramount chiefs of a number of important iwi, especially within Tainui. Several major iwi do not adhere to the movement, notably Tūhoe, Ngāti Porou and Ngāpuhi. David Rankin of Ngāpuhi argues that the monarch is not the king of all Māori, and that a claim to such a title diminishes the rangatiratanga and mana of iwi not associated with the movement.

The monarch is appointed by the leaders of the iwi involved on the day of the previous monarch's funeral. In principle the position is not hereditary, but every monarch since Pōtatau has been the child of the previous one. The Kauhanganui acts as the Kīngitanga and Waikato Tainui parliament. A coronation celebration, the Koroneihana, is held each year at Tūrangawaewae, and the poukai, begun by Tāwhiao in the 1880s, is an annual circuit of royal visits to supporting marae.

In 2014 King Tūheitia established an honours system outside the New Zealand and Commonwealth governments, with three orders bearing the motto Ko te mana motuhake, "The self-determination and control over one's own destiny". Charles III became the first member of the Order of King Pootatau Te Wherowhero in 2023. The Kīngitanga's own tartan was registered with the Scottish Register of Tartans in 2015.

summary: The Māori King movement, the Kīngitanga, grew from 1850s meetings of North Island iwi seeking unity against the sale of land, and crowned Pōtatau Te Wherowhero in 1858. The invasion of the Waikato and land confiscations followed; today the monarchy operates outside New Zealand law.
references: Ranginui Walker, Ka Whawhai Tonu Matou: Struggle Without End (Penguin, 1990)
notes: Start 1853 (circa) follows the article's revival of the rūnanga 'around 1853'; the article says the movement arose in the 1850s and the first king was crowned in 1858.
The article says the monarch is a 'parliamentary elective monarchy since 1890', but dates the Kauhanganui to 1892 at Maungakawa; the 1890 date is left out.

The article calls Wiremu Tamihana 'Tamihana' and 'Wiremu Tamihana'; Tāmihana Te Rauparaha is a separate person in the article but both are described as proposing the kingdom (one in the background, one the kingmaker); kept as the article has them.
The article's bibliography names only Walker, Ranginui (1990), Ka Whawhai Tonu Matou (Penguin); references left empty as instructed.
Te Rata's age at coronation is given as 'between 30 and 33'; left out. The Matutaera/Mahuta lines on the Mahuta Tāwhiao handover to a brother in 1903 to 1910 were left out for length.
The article is inconsistent in spelling (Tūheitia/Tuheitia, Pootatau/Pōtatau); the macron forms are used except in the order's name.
